Portable hydrokinetic turbine for 0.5-1.0 m/s streams: low-flow redesign (v4)

Scope and status. Everything in this package is model prediction and design intent. No part has been printed, machined or tested; no GL60 has been measured; manufacturer web pages (cubemars.com, genasun, bluerobotics.com, digikey) could not be reached from this session, so the generator values are the ones listed in the brief and in the earlier review, bracketed by sensitivity cases. Every number below is written by docs/make_report_v4.py from the result files of the scripts in model/, cad/ and tools/.

1. Executive summary and feasibility verdict

  • What the GL60 can deliver (model, baseline assumptions, arrangement A, buck-boost MPPT): net 12 V electrical power 0.16 W at 0.5 m/s, 0.49 W at 0.6, 0.98 W at 0.7, 1.65 W at 0.8, 3.60 W at 1.0 m/s (12.8 W at 1.5, 29.5 W at 2.0). Honest band: -30 % / +10 % (hydrofoil polars at Re 4e4-8e4 from an XFOIL surrogate, unmeasured friction and generator constants; section 8). Over a 24 h day at 0.6-0.8 m/s that is roughly 12-40 Wh: enough to keep a phone or a headlamp charged, not a camp power supply.
  • Minimum flow. The rotor sustains rotation and the converter accepts power from 0.5 m/s (the 5 V minimum input of the converter and the fixed friction are the limiters; at 0.4 m/s the bus would be below 5 V and the net output negative). Self-start is model-marginal at 0.5 m/s: 0.4 m/s (optimistic) / 0.5 (baseline) / 0.6 (pessimistic), set by the assumed GL60 cogging (24 mN m peak) plus seal and bearing breakaway. Gates G1 and G6 of the test plan decide it.
  • The winding resistance is not the obstacle. At these powers the torque is tens of mN m, so copper loss is 0.1-3.5 % of the available hydraulic power below 1 m/s. The obstacles are, in order: rotor efficiency at Reynolds numbers of 4e4-8e4 (Cp 0.25-0.33), the fixed friction torque (seal + bearing + motor no-load, 7 mN m plus no-load loss), the generator voltage (only 5.1 V at 0.5 m/s: a boost-capable converter is mandatory; a rectifier straight into the battery produces nothing below 0.4 m/s), and the converter's own minimum input voltage and quiescent draw.
  • A gearbox does not help. A 2:1 or 3:1 stage (optimistic 96 % per stage, +5 mN m) changes net output by -22 % at 0.5 m/s and -1 % at 1.0 m/s with the real converter: rejected; direct drive is kept.
  • Selected rotor: 3 blades, NACA 4412 blending to NACA 4418 at the root, Schmitz planform for design TSR 2.0 scaled x1.3, root chord 49.8 mm, maximum chord 57.8 mm, tip chord 31.0 mm, root twist 31.3 deg, solidity 0.39; it runs at TSR 3.0-3.4 (130-320 rpm over 0.5-1.0 m/s). Against the previous 1-2 m/s blade on its drum hub it delivers 2.8x at 0.6 m/s and 1.47x at 1.0 m/s; against the original rev-2 blade placed on the same small hub it gains +745 % at 0.5, +35 % at 0.6, +13 % at 0.7 and -0 % at 1.0 m/s: the gain is where the brief asks for it, and the two blades are equivalent above 0.9 m/s.
  • Recommended mounting: arrangement A (rotor on a short 316 shaft ahead of a stationary sealed nacelle). The hub radius drops from 48 to 28 mm, which is worth +83 % at 0.7 m/s and +48 % at 1.0 m/s against the same blade in the hub-integrated drum (B), and the 8 mm seal halves the seal friction. The price is depth: 141 mm operating, which packs as two pieces of 58 mm (rotor) and 75 mm (nacelle) by removing one M4 screw. The 76 mm target is met packed, not operating.

3. Optimisation methodology and objective function

  1. Polars (model/polars.py): NeuralFoil (XFOIL surrogate, Ncrit 9) on a 29 x 10 (alpha, Re) grid for NACA 4412 / 4415 / 4418, SG6043, E387, FX63-137 and E818, Viterna-extended to +-90 deg for the standstill estimate. E387 (confidence 0.84) and E818 (0.64, coarse database coordinates) are reported but not selectable. Experimental polars at Re 4e4-8e4 are not available to this project.
  2. BEM (model/bem_lowflow.py): Prandtl tip and hub losses, Buhl high-induction correction, per-element Reynolds number, root blend to the 18 % thick section over the inner 35 % of span, nacelle inflow deficit factor 0.85 inboard of r 38 mm for arrangement A (assumption), vectorised Ning residual solved by bisection. Cross-checks: the near-inviscid limit stays below Betz (Cp 0.43 with tip/hub losses), P = omega Q, and the v3.1 blade evaluated with both the old analytic polar and the new tables agrees within the expected 10-20 % (the thick root is the difference).
  3. Coupled operating point (model/generator_lowflow.py): rotor torque curve against friction (seal, bearing, motor no-load, hub windage) and the generator (KV 21.5, Kt 0.444 N m/A, R 5.5 ohm, L 2.72 mH, 14 pole pairs, Schottky bridge 2 x Vf(I), commutation overlap as a reactive voltage drop), then the converter (efficiency eta_max - k/P_in, quiescent draw, minimum input voltage, and either a boost-with-clamp or a buck-boost input window). The MPPT law picks the bus voltage (= rotor speed) that maximises converter output inside the window; it never commands more than the 1.35 A rating. Standstill torque uses alpha = 90 deg - twist on every element with W = V (no induction) and the Viterna polars; breakaway = cogging + seal + bearing breakaway. Dynamic friction and breakaway are separate.
  4. Objective: J = sum over V of w(V) P_net(V) with P_net = 0 where the candidate cannot self-start, cannot sustain rotation along the unloaded path to its operating point, or sits below the converter's 5 V input. Two weightings: uniform over 0.5-1.0 m/s (six flows) and low-flow-weighted {0.5: 0.3, 0.6: 0.3, 0.7: 0.2, 0.8: 0.1, 0.9: 0.05, 1.0: 0.05} (illustrative, not measured). Also tracked: the same without the self-start gate ("hand-started") and with cogging 8 / 40 mN m.
  5. Design space (model/optimize_blades.py): stage 1 = 384 candidates: 2 / 3 / 4 / 5 blades x four airfoils x design TSR 1.5-6 (Schmitz planform at the airfoil's best-L/D angle at the local Reynolds number) x chord scale 0.7 / 1.0 / 1.3 (chord capped at 60 mm). Stage 2 = 80 refinements around the leader (TSR 1.75-2.5, chord scale 1.3-1.7, chord cap 60 / 68, pitch -3 / 0 / +3 deg, two-blade and SG6043 checks). Selection: the mean of the two normalised objectives, subject to self-start at 0.5 m/s under baseline cogging and a root chord <= 52 mm (the three pockets must leave printable walls on the 28 mm hub); ties go to the lower solidity.

Reading. Two blades give the best Cp per unit solidity but cannot self-start below 0.6 m/s; four and five blades start earlier but lose Cp to profile drag at these Reynolds numbers. Design TSR 2-2.5 wins because the wide chords raise the local Reynolds number (the chord is the only lever on Re at a given flow) and the standstill torque, while the actual Cp peak still sits at TSR 3-3.5 and the coupled MPPT point at TSR 2.8-3.4, where the GL60's voltage is highest for the torque it must absorb. The low-Reynolds sections lose in the coupled result despite their better 2-D L/D: their higher design lift coefficient produces narrower chords (lower Re) and a sharper Cp peak. The objective surface is flat near the optimum (the top eight stage-2 candidates are within 1.5 % of each other), so the root-chord packaging limit decided the final pick without a measurable performance cost (98.3 % of the best low-flow score).

5. Selected blade geometry and why it won

3 blades, NACA 4412 outboard blending to NACA 4418 over the inner 35 % (printability and root bending), Schmitz planform at design TSR 2.0 x1.3 (capped at 60 mm), root eased to 85 % at the hub, elliptical tip taper to 55 %, pitch offset +0 deg, 1.0 mm blunt trailing edge. Station data: model/selected_design.json (chord 49.8 -> 57.8 -> 31.0 mm; twist 31.3 -> 7.2 deg). Figures 5 and 6 compare it with the previous designs. It won because it (i) self-starts at 0.5 m/s under the baseline cogging while the two-blade and the TSR >= 3 designs do not, (ii) has the highest coupled output at 0.5-0.7 m/s (Re effect of the wide chord), (iii) matches the original rev-2 blade above 0.9 m/s, and (iv) still fits three pockets on a 28 mm hub. What it gives up: about 5 % at 2.0 m/s against the rev-2 blade and a higher standstill drag (thrust at 2 m/s 49 N at the operating point).

Load control. Below the clamp voltage both converters regulate the bus, i.e. the rotor speed, so the generator cannot stall the rotor: the equilibrium sits on the stable side of the torque peak (fig. 9). With the boost-only converter the bus is clamped at the battery above about 1.25 m/s; the rotor is then held at a fixed speed and, from about 1.75 m/s, the clamp current exceeds the GL60 rating: a boost-only unit needs a 1.5-2 A limiter or a 40 V relay dump for the 1-2 m/s survivability case. The buck-boost keeps regulating to 2 m/s (1.20 A at 26.3 V). Open circuit at 2 m/s is 54 V: below the 60 V TVS standoff and the converter's 60 V input. Current and temperature: copper loss at 2 m/s is 7.9 W inside a sealed nacelle; the brief's 0.5-1.0 m/s duty is < 0.1 W. Thermal limits are not the sizing case below 1.5 m/s; the earlier v3.1 heat-path analysis applies if the device is left in a 2 m/s flow (rear cap in 6061).

7. Recommended compact mounting and waterproofing (arrangement A), with B quantified

A: rotor on a short shaft, stationary nacelle behind B: hub-integrated (v3.1 drum rotor)
hub radius / ratio 28 mm / 0.28 48.2 mm / 0.47 (the GL60 inside a 3 in drum)
net W at 0.5 / 0.7 / 1.0 m/s (same blade) 0.16 / 0.98 / 3.60 0.00 / 0.54 / 2.44
rotary seal one 8 mm PTFE lip seal (run 4 mN m assumed) one 15 mm PTFE lip seal (7.5 mN m)
bearings one 608-2RS in the cap + the GL60's own two 6702-2RS
machined parts shaft, front cap, rear cap, tube ends (4) spindle, 2 caps, split ring, plug, boss, 3 struts, tube ends (9+)
waterproof boundary tube + 1 O-ring per cap + lip seal + WetLink + vent tube + O-rings + lip seal + potting plug
operating depth 141 mm; packs as 58 + 75 mm 73 mm
flow obstruction behind the rotor 3 in nacelle (14 % of the disc area), modelled as a 15 % inflow deficit inboard of r 38 mm none beyond the drum itself
seal service pull the hub (one screw), press the seal from the wet face partial disassembly (v3.1 plan)

Load path (A, fig. 10a). Thrust: blade -> airfoil tongue (clamped between the two hub halves by an axial M3) -> hub -> collar A -> shaft -> collar B -> 608 inner race -> outer race -> front-cap floor -> cap plug and flange -> tube -> clamp -> three L-struts -> guard ring and stake. Reverse load: DIN 471-8 circlip behind the bearing (0.2 mm end play); the seal pressed in front of the bearing retains the outer race. Torque: hub D-bore -> shaft D-flat -> cross-pinned dog hub -> TPU disc (two dogs, 0.2 mm radial clearance) -> GL60 bell; the stator is screwed to the rear cap. The GL60 carries no rotor thrust and no radial load. The motor is dry: tube, one EPDM O-ring per cap, an 8 mm PTFE lip seal on the polished 316 journal, a WetLink M10 penetrator and an M6 vent; IP45 is irrelevant inside that boundary. Penalties quantified: the seal and bearing take 7 mN m of the 38 mN m the rotor makes at 0.5 m/s (19 %) and 4 % at 1.0 m/s; the nacelle inflow deficit costs about 3 % of Cp (assumption, to be checked in G8/G11); the hub ratio 0.28 costs the annulus area shown in the feasibility table.

9. Reproducible source code and CAD exports

model/polars.py (polar tables), bem_lowflow.py, generator_lowflow.py, feasibility.py, optimize_blades.py (stages 1-2 and the selection), coupled_eval.py (figures 2-9, comparison, sensitivities); cad/make_v4.py (parametric assembly, STEP per part, assembly STEP, print-oriented STLs with the blade meshed as a closed structured surface), cad/views_v4.py (figure 10); tools/qa_gates_v4.py. Exports: out/v4_assembly.step, out/v4_*.step (28 parts, 11 printed, 4 machined), out/v4_*_PRINT.stl (11 files, all closed, blade mesh within 0.13 % of its STEP volume, tilted -4.3 deg for a level pressure face). Regenerate in the order given in README.md. Print notes: blades pressure-side down with tree supports under the leading-edge overhang, 100 % infill, layers along the span; hub halves parting face down, no supports; TPU disc flat; clamp halves flat; ring as three arcs. Minimum blade thickness 3.7 mm at the tip (12 % of 31.0 mm), 1.0 mm trailing edge. Structural check (2 m/s survival, 1171 rpm open circuit): root bending 0.57 N m of torque shared by three roots and 16.4 N thrust per blade at 72 mm lever -> under 2 MPa in the 12 %-thick root section (in-plane for a flat print; allowable 15 MPa short-term).

11. Practical prototype testing plan

See docs/TEST_PLAN_v4.md (12 gates). The four measurements that close the model, in order of their effect on the 0.5-0.7 m/s prediction: G1 generator constants and cogging, G2 breakaway and running friction of the sealed shaft, G6 standstill torque of the printed rotor, G8 the power curve in a real stream.

12. Bill of materials for the simplest working prototype

docs/BOM_v4.csv: 29 lines, roughly $3,189-3,550 of parts beyond the GL60 (converter choice dominates; machining prices are estimates for a job shop; no anodising, battery, cable beyond 3 m or instrumentation). The four machined parts (shaft, two caps, tube ends) are the only non-printed, non-COTS items.

14. Unresolved assumptions

  • GL60: KV / Kt / R convention, cogging torque (the single biggest unknown for self-start), no-load loss, lead exit, which hole pattern is the stator's.
  • Hydrofoil polars at Re 4e4-8e4 come from an XFOIL surrogate; wind-tunnel data for printed-rough surfaces would likely sit 10-30 % lower in L/D.
  • The standstill torque model (Viterna post-stall, no induction) is the least validated part of the BEM; it decides the self-start verdict.
  • Seal and bearing friction (assumed from diameter scaling of catalogue-class values), converter efficiency curve and minimum input voltage, quiescent draw.
  • Nacelle inflow deficit (15 % inboard of r 38 mm), guard-ring and shallow-water effects (G11), turbulence and debris.
  • Manufacturer pages were unreachable: WetLink, Genasun GVB-8, LT8390 modules and seal part numbers must be confirmed before ordering.
